rationale: Uncertainty: HIGH. The dossier is entirely blank — the Firebase web app URL provides no identifying information about the project's purpose, communities, or mechanism. I apply the underdog protection floor given the absence of documentation, but this is an abstention in all but formality.

name: Consciousness Evolution Operating System (ConSoc)
rationale: The dossier for ConSoc is almost entirely blank — tagline 'Feel Symbiotic Cooperation' and civic technology practitioners as beneficiaries is all I have to work with. The constitution requires me to apply underdog protection for completeness below 0.4, and the floor of 30 applies. I cannot make any substantive scoring judgment about this project.

name: We Live It
rationale: AI-powered community-driven urban planning is a domain I value, but the dossier is almost empty — even the primary_users_or_beneficiaries field appears broken. I apply the underdog floor of 30 because completeness is below 0.4. I cannot assess whether this is a genuinely empowering tool or a commercial AI platform using community engagement language without substance.

name: Aragon
rationale: M6 applied: DAO governance for VC-backed crypto entities; token holders not excluded populations; Polychain/Dragonfly/Consensys backing; limited civic relevance

name: Open Data Editor (ODE)
rationale: Open Data Editor makes tabular data validation accessible to non-technical actors in civil society and government — a genuine democratisation of data quality. The Global South deployment earns C2 credit. The M6 reduction reflects the tool's framing as technical data hygiene rather than engaging with the political questions of why certain data standards are adopted and whose knowledge gets counted as valid.

name: Civic Tech Field Guide
rationale: Explicitly acknowledges Western bias and limited Global South representation as core limitation; strongest honest C4 self-examination of type; underdog_signal; FNF funding

name: openparliament.ca
rationale: openparliament.ca makes Canadian parliamentary activity searchable by individual, making political accountability more accessible to citizens and researchers. The individual/grassroots maintainer gives it genuine C5 underdog credibility. What limits the score is the informs democratic depth — users can search what their representatives said, but the tool gives them no mechanism to influence what happens next.

name: FixMyStreet
rationale: FixMyStreet addresses citizen-council accountability gaps in street maintenance — a real if relatively low-stakes power asymmetry. What limits the score is that the mechanism is informational (report a problem) rather than structural (guarantee a response), coverage varies significantly by local authority, and there is no evidence that the design examined which communities are systematically excluded from reporting or receiving responses.

name: WriteToThem
rationale: Making it easier to contact elected representatives is a genuine democratic access mechanism, particularly for people unfamiliar with the political system. The limitation that defines the score is that WriteToThem cannot guarantee or even track responsive rates from elected officials, which means the tool improves access to the mechanism without examining whether that mechanism is itself responsive to ordinary constituents relative to organized interests.

name: Local Intelligence Hub
rationale: Data for climate campaigners to demonstrate public mandate to MPs is useful organizing infrastructure, but the beneficiaries — campaigners and organizers — are already-organized civic actors rather than communities excluded from political processes. The members-only restriction and variable dataset currency limit both the transparency of the tool and the ability to assess its equity impacts.

name: Constitute Project
rationale: Constitutional database used in high-stakes design processes; documents limitation of focusing on written documents over informal practices; researchers/courts not excluded populations; NED/OSF/Google.org funding

name: Moral Machine
rationale: Ethical AI crowdsourcing; moderate C3+C4; but limited direct community empowerment or excluded population centering

name: Open Letter
rationale: Open Letter facilitates open letter campaigns with documented outcomes like making a Brussels avenue car-free. This is consults level democratic engagement — expressing collective views to decision-makers without binding them to respond. The generic civic beneficiary framing and absence of any self-examination of whether open letter campaigns reach beyond already-engaged civic participants limits the score.

name: Tech Coops List
rationale: The Tech Coops List documents an alternative model of technology production where workers own the means — directly relevant to my interest in intra-class dynamics and who benefits from digital labour. But this is an information resource rather than a mechanism that redistributes power within the tech sector; the directory format limits the democratic depth score.

name: Internet Archive Wayback Machine
rationale: The Internet Archive preserves the historical record against institutional erasure, which is a genuine epistemic power asymmetry correction — governments and corporations can unpublish evidence, but the Archive provides persistent public access. I flag high popularity risk. The primary limitation is that the Archive operates as a passive repository rather than an active contestability mechanism.

name: TheyWorkForYou
rationale: Parliamentary transparency is a genuine democratic need and TheyWorkForYou does it well, but the primary limitation is that making voting records accessible informs citizens without giving them any mechanism to act on that information. The score reflects a solid information asymmetry correction without the structural contestability that would lift it higher.

name: Campaign Tracker
rationale: Political advertising spend transparency in Dutch elections with documented policy impact (2023 electoral law changes) is a genuine accountability mechanism. What limits the higher bracket is that journalists and researchers benefit more directly than the voters who are the nominal targets of the advertising — the accountability circuit runs through professional intermediaries rather than directly empowering affected communities.

name: OpenSanctions
rationale: Open source sanctions and PEP data is useful investigative infrastructure, but the primary beneficiaries — compliance professionals, financial institutions, investigators — are professional and institutional actors rather than populations affected by the sanctioned individuals' actions. The documented LLM error issues and human moderation requirements show methodological honesty.

name: Full Fact AI
rationale: M4 applied: AI processing 333k sentences/day with limited transparency on algorithmic decision-making; fact-checkers not excluded populations; strong deployment record; Google/Facebook/Omidyar/NED funding

name: youtube-dl
rationale: HIGH pop_risk: infrastructure tool without equity mandate; some C5 underdog signal from copyright battles

name: In The News
rationale: Volunteer-driven Wikipedia news section; documents Western/coverage bias as limitation; general public as primary users; limited governance depth; Wikimedia Foundation

name: Digital Account Management Toolkit
rationale: Nonprofit account security for civil society; civil society as indirect beneficiaries; limited excluded population focus; Digital Charity Lab; UK/Ireland only

name: GrantNav
rationale: Funding transparency tool; moderate C1+C4; limited community participation design

name: JOSS
rationale: Open source academic publishing; moderate C3+C4; limited excluded population centering

name: Open Access – Transparency International UK
rationale: Open Access TI UK provided beneficial ownership transparency data that supported civil society advocacy on corporate accountability. The platform appears to be offline as of 2026, raising sustainability questions, and the primary beneficiaries (journalists, compliance professionals) are several removes from the communities harmed by financial opacity.

name: Parse The Bill
rationale: Parse The Bill reduces the complexity barrier to understanding UK parliamentary legislation — a useful information equity function. The AI-accuracy caveat is honestly stated. What it doesn't address is the structural inequality of who can act on understanding a bill: the legislative participation gap is about access to institutional power, not just bill comprehension.

name: Spartacus
rationale: Spartacus's conditional commitment mechanism is interesting as a collective action solution, but the dossier gives no evidence of who is using it, what problems it is solving, or whether it actually helps excluded communities overcome collective action barriers rather than helping already-organised groups coordinate more efficiently.

name: Mastodon C
rationale: Data science and analytics consultancy for open data and civic technology is infrastructure-level work that enables other accountability mechanisms. The documented policy contributions (UK open data standards, EU data governance) show genuine impact. The score is limited by the professional service model — the direct beneficiaries are government and civil society clients.

name: Who Posted What?
rationale: A grassroots investigative tool enabling fact-checkers to search Facebook content for public interest work — the individual authorship and access restrictions demonstrate both structural disadvantage (high C5) and methodological care (access limited to verified public interest workers). The score is primarily driven by the underdog signal and the genuine epistemic accountability function.

name: Open Supply Hub
rationale: Open Supply Hub's global supply chain mapping creates transparency that advocacy organisations can use to pressure brands on worker conditions. The M2 reduction reflects my concern that the data flows primarily to brands and retailers rather than to the workers in those facilities — transparency enabling better institutional management of supply chains is not the same as transparency that gives workers power over their conditions.

name: Frankenstein Bill
rationale: Legislative transparency tool; moderate C5 underdog signal; limited participatory design

name: Find Local Consultations
rationale: Government consultation access tool; moderate C1+C6; limited community engagement design

name: Remember to Vote
rationale: Remember to Vote addresses a specific participation barrier — voter ID requirements creating confusion about polling station logistics — with a free SMS reminder service. This is informs level democratic engagement: reminding people of a right they already have rather than addressing why some communities participate less in elections.

name: The Government Says
rationale: The Government Says aggregates UK government press releases in real time — a monitoring tool that reduces information asymmetry between government communications professionals and those tracking official messaging. This is primarily useful for journalists and researchers; the community-driven governance is noted but the tool sits firmly at the informs level.

name: Bluesky Social
rationale: M6 applied: VC-backed consumer social app without explicit equity mandate; pop_risk HIGH; Sequoia/Benchmark/Khosla backing; general public as primary users limit C2

name: Docs Plus
rationale: Open-source collaborative docs with community_ownership; thin dossier reduces confidence; Grant for Web/Nesta; limited excluded population focus

name: Logos
rationale: Privacy/censorship resistance tool; moderate C1; limited community centering; HIGH uncertainty from low completeness

name: Members' Interests
rationale: Parliamentary accountability tool; moderate C1+C4; 404 access; HIGH uncertainty

name: OpenBudgets.eu
rationale: OpenBudgets.eu made EU budget data more accessible and analysable — a transparency function for fiscal accountability. At informs level democratic depth, this serves analysts rather than giving affected communities any formal mechanism to contest budget allocations.

name: Turbo Phonebank
rationale: Turbo Phonebank is a free grassroots tool for campaign canvassing that lowers the resource barrier for volunteer-driven advocacy. The single-maintainer structure earns C5 credit. The beneficiaries are campaigners and organisers, who are not structurally excluded in the sense this constitution rewards most highly.

name: Violation Tracker UK
rationale: A database of corporate violations and enforcement actions is useful accountability infrastructure, but the thin dossier (JS required to access the database) limits what I can assess. The information is primarily useful to researchers and journalists rather than the workers or communities harmed by the violations.

name: CKAN
rationale: Government open data management infrastructure without explicit equity mandate; pop_risk HIGH as global government data standard; UK/World Bank/EU Commission backing; researchers/government not excluded populations

name: Sugartrail
rationale: Corporate network analysis; moderate C5 underdog signal; limited community engagement

name: Kialo
rationale: Structured debate platform; moderate C6; limited excluded population focus

name: DemTech Navigator
rationale: Democratic technology navigator; moderate C4; academic framing limits community centering

name: Citizens Advice Tableau Public Profile
rationale: Citizens Advice's data visualisations track client demographics and advice issues — the underlying data is about people facing financial difficulty, housing problems, and benefit denials. But the visualisations serve researchers and policymakers rather than the affected clients; there is no documented mechanism for the data to feed back into service improvement co-designed with clients.

name: Go Vocal
rationale: A commercial government engagement platform with some documentation of community consultation outcomes. I apply M4 at moderate magnitude because the proprietary algorithm for AI analysis lacks transparency, which is precisely the governance gap I look for in tools used to synthesize public participation data — the translation from community input to policy recommendation is hidden inside a commercial product.

name: OA.Report
rationale: Open access reporting tool; moderate C1+C4; academic infrastructure without community focus

name: OSINT Framework
rationale: OSINT Framework provides a curated toolkit for open source intelligence gathering — primarily useful for journalists, investigators, and security researchers. The individual/grassroots maintenance and thin documentation earn C5 credit. The tool is neutral infrastructure that could serve investigative accountability as easily as surveillance.

name: The List
rationale: The List is a single-person resource tracking UK trust and foundation funding changes — genuinely useful for cash-strapped small charities navigating the funding ecosystem. The reliance on community-submitted data and honest sustainability concerns earn it C5 credit. This is primarily institutional information flow rather than a power correction for the communities that the charities serve.

name: MyActionCenter
rationale: Activist coordination tools for organized campaigns have value in the democratic infrastructure, but the primary users — nonprofits and political organizations — are already-organized actors, and the tool requires NationBuilder platform access with associated fees.

name: Parallel Parliament
rationale: Parliamentary tracking with live transcripts and bill amendment tracking is useful civic infrastructure for researchers and policy professionals. The underdog signal for a small commercial startup is real. The primary limitation is that the beneficiaries are professionals and researchers rather than communities excluded from political processes.

name: WhatGov
rationale: Parliament, Clearly — a useful simplification layer on parliamentary information, but the sparse dossier and generic citizen framing prevent a higher score. The tool informs rather than empowers, and there is no documented engagement with how it reaches communities excluded from political processes by literacy, language, or digital access barriers.

name: Public Editor
rationale: Collaborative fact-checking has epistemic accountability value, but the sparse dossier prevents a full assessment. The beneficiaries (journalists, media organizations, readers) are primarily professional and engaged civic actors. There is no evidence of community engagement with the tool's design or critical examination of whether collaborative fact-checking redistributes epistemic authority or consolidates it in media institutions.

name: Wikum
rationale: Collective summarization of large online discussions is an interesting deliberative infrastructure tool. The academic context limits the evidence base for real-world deployment and community impact. The score reflects genuine democratic depth potential without evidence that this has been deployed at scale with excluded populations.

name: EDGAR
rationale: M6 applied: technical CLI tool for SEC data retrieval; journalists/researchers not excluded populations; Bellingcat backing; no community governance dimension

name: Contracts for Data Collaboration
rationale: M6 applied: academic data governance framework document; researchers/policymakers as users; Berkman Klein/Mozilla/NSF funding; technical framing without community engagement

name: Fatebook
rationale: M6 applied: prediction market framing treats civic information as optimisation problem; researchers/forecasters not excluded populations; Open Philanthropy/SFF funding; LLC governance

name: Nym
rationale: Privacy network infrastructure; moderate C1; limited community centering and participatory design

name: Plinth
rationale: AI platform for measuring community impact and managing government programs has genuine infrastructure value for charities and local authorities. The HAF programme management use-case is concrete. What limits the score is that the direct beneficiaries are organizations (charities, funders) rather than communities, and there is no evidence that the platform critically examines whether its measurement frameworks capture what matters to the communities being served.

name: Vote for Policies
rationale: Blind policy comparison for voters is a genuinely useful epistemic tool for reducing tribal voting. The project is now discontinued after the 2024 election. The underdog signal for a nonprofit tool that shut down is real. The primary limitation is that informing voters without examining which communities have least access to policy information leaves the structural question unanswered.

name: GovTrack.us
rationale: US congressional tracking with voting records and legislative data is a solid transparency platform, but the beneficiaries — citizens, journalists, advocates — are primarily already-engaged civic actors. The score reflects information asymmetry correction without structural power redistribution or community-centring.

name: CharmVerse
rationale: M6 applied: web3 community platform for DAO operators; DAO operators not excluded populations; Coinbase Ventures/Polychain backing; no civic governance dimension

name: Harmonica
rationale: M4 applied: AI collecting/synthesising stakeholder views without transparent governance for data use; reduces score from raw 25.6

name: NumFOCUS
rationale: Open source scientific computing; moderate C3; limited political/equity framing

name: Open Council Data UK
rationale: Open Council Data UK provides structured data on UK councillor compositions — useful for researchers and campaigners tracking political representation. The for-profit structure and researcher/campaigner beneficiary framing positions this firmly in the data infrastructure space without engaging with the communities underrepresented in the councils being tracked.

name: Open Science Framework
rationale: OSF improves research transparency and reproducibility — important for the quality of public knowledge, but primarily valuable to researchers, funders, and institutions. The popularity risk flag reflects OSF's well-established position in research infrastructure. The generic beneficiary framing and absent community engagement limit scoring; this is not a disadvantaged project.

name: PostBug
rationale: PostBug enables postcard campaigns to power — a simple tactile advocacy tool. The dossier is thin on evidence of actual use, outcomes, or excluded population targeting. This is a facilitation tool at consults level: it makes expressing opposition or support easier but does nothing structural about whether decision-makers respond.

name: Shareyourpaper.org
rationale: Shareyourpaper.org helps researchers legally deposit their papers for open access — an important compliance support tool. The benefit flows primarily to researchers and to readers in under-resourced institutions. This is a smoother version of an existing pathway rather than a mechanism that challenges the structural incentives maintaining the paywall publishing model.

name: UrbanistAI
rationale: UrbanistAI's AI-powered participatory planning raises exactly the concern from my SKEPSIS work: collective intelligence framing that could function as a legitimacy tactic for planning decisions already made. The documented absence of any independent evaluation, AI bias transparency, or methodology publication is precisely what M4 penalises.

name: Spacetube
rationale: Spacetube's group-to-group Matrix chat enables inter-group communication without both groups needing to share a server — a useful feature for distributed organising. The underdog signal earns C5 credit. Without evidence of who uses it, what communities it serves, or any power analysis, this is infrastructure of uncertain impact.

name: OpenOrigins
rationale: Content authentication to combat deepfakes addresses a real epistemic power asymmetry in visual media. The sparse dossier prevents a full assessment. The primary beneficiaries are journalists and media organizations; there is no evidence of engagement with communities most affected by deepfake-based disinformation, and no self-examination of whether authentication tools centralize verification authority in institutions.

name: Agencies for Good
rationale: A network of tech-for-good agencies and freelancers is infrastructure for civic technology supply rather than demand — it helps build better tools rather than directly addressing power asymmetries. The cooperative governance model is a genuine structural signal. The score is limited by the professional-sector beneficiaries.

name: Shared Digital Guides
rationale: Guides for nonprofits to use digital tools for social good has infrastructure value for the charity sector. The score is limited by the professional-sector focus and acknowledged absence of a formal evidence base for impact.

name: Theft Bisect
rationale: Theft Bisect is a clever individual tool addressing a specific institutional policy (British Transport Police's footage review limit), and the honest acknowledgement of GDPR concerns shows some critical awareness. The M6 reduction reflects the primarily technical framing — this addresses an efficiency problem rather than examining the structural relationship between policing, surveillance infrastructure, and who bears the costs of bike theft in different communities.

name: Charity Digital Skills Report
rationale: M6 applied: annual informational survey of sector professionals; charity professionals not excluded populations; Media Trust project; no community empowerment

name: Global Fact-Check Bot
rationale: M4 applied: AI fact-checking expanding epistemic authority without clear governance for contested claims

name: MapIt
rationale: Geographic boundary API; limited equity or community framing; mySociety infrastructure tool

name: Metaculus
rationale: Prediction market platform; limited excluded population focus or community empowerment

name: Nestr
rationale: Organisational governance tool; limited evidence of excluded population centering

name: ORCID
rationale: ORCID solves a real attribution problem in research infrastructure, and the effort to monitor adoption disparities across regions and disciplines is noted. But this is infrastructure serving researchers and institutions, not excluded populations; the power asymmetries it addresses (author disambiguation, citation attribution) are internal to the research system rather than structural exclusions with civic consequences.

name: Open Data Communities
rationale: Open Data Communities published important datasets on deprivation, housing, and planning — data that underpins much civic research. The announced discontinuation in March 2025 means this is infrastructure being withdrawn. The government institutional origin limits C5; the observational methodology and researcher beneficiaries limit C2 and C3.

name: Timecounts
rationale: Timecounts is a volunteer management platform for nonprofits and community organisations. No mechanism for excluded community voice in design or governance.

name: Discourse
rationale: Forum software with community management features. The primary beneficiaries are tech companies and product teams, not communities facing structural exclusion. Discourse enables conversation but is primarily serving resource-rich organizations — the documented challenges around moderation at scale and technical expertise requirements mean it is less accessible to community organizations with limited technical capacity.

name: Collaborative Data Patterns
rationale: M6 applied: technical ODI guidebook for data practitioners; data practitioners not excluded populations; Open Data Institute project; purely informational

name: DAO Governance Surfaces
rationale: M6 applied: technical blockchain analysis without community engagement framing

name: Radicle
rationale: Radicle's peer-to-peer sovereign code forge addresses developer dependency on centralised platforms — a real digital sovereignty concern. The M6 reduction reflects that the technical framing of platform independence doesn't engage with the governance questions of who benefits from open source infrastructure and who is structurally excluded from participating in it.

name: Viewpoints
rationale: AI-powered polls and consensus building for meetings and events. The absence of any published research on poll accuracy or bias, combined with undocumented AI methodology, makes it impossible to assess whether the consensus mechanisms are actually representative or reflect algorithmic artifacts. I apply M6 weakly for the technical framing that doesn't engage with governance dimensions.

name: semanticClimate
rationale: semanticClimate provides semantic search over climate science literature — a research accessibility tool. No community engagement and no mechanism that changes who can participate in climate policy debates.

name: UK Parliament Developer Portal
rationale: M6 applied: technical API portal for parliamentary data; developers not excluded populations; government-operated; dead_link at scrape time

name: Pear by Holepunch
rationale: M6 applied: technical p2p platform for app developers; developers not excluded populations; experimental modules documented as limitation; VC-funded

name: Pageviews Analysis
rationale: Pageviews Analysis tracks Wikipedia attention metrics — useful for researchers and editors understanding public interest patterns. The individual/grassroots maintenance earns C5 credit. The tool has no civic power asymmetry dimension and no connection to excluded populations.

name: Plausible Analytics
rationale: Plausible Analytics provides privacy-respecting website analytics — an important digital rights tool for website operators. The beneficiaries are website operators, not communities facing exclusion; this is a market substitution for a surveillance product rather than a structural power redistribution.

name: River Sentiment Dashboard
rationale: The River Sentiment Dashboard visualises social media sentiment alongside ecological data for Thames basin rivers — an interesting methodological combination. The tool is primarily academic research infrastructure; there is no mechanism for communities along the rivers to shape assessment of their waterways or use the data to hold polluters accountable.

name: Open Standards for Data Guidebook
rationale: The ODI's guidebook helps practitioners develop and adopt open data standards — valuable technical infrastructure. This operates entirely within the professional civic tech ecosystem and doesn't engage with the communities most affected by how data about them is standardised and shared.

name: MP Twitter Bios
rationale: A narrow academic research tool examining MP self-presentation on Twitter — whether MPs mention their party affiliation. This is interesting research but has limited structural impact on power asymmetries or excluded populations.

name: UK Policy Dojo
rationale: M6 applied: AI-only policy deliberation bypassing democratic governance

name: Gapminder Worldview Upgrader
rationale: Correcting misconceptions about global development is epistemically valuable but raises the question I bring from SKEPSIS: whose misconceptions are being corrected, towards whose framing of development? The adoption by Fortune 500 companies and educational institutions suggests this tool may function more as legitimacy infrastructure for development sector actors than as structural power redistribution for communities represented in the data. I apply M6 because the technical quiz format frames attitude change as a neutral educational intervention.

name: GOV.UK Forms
rationale: Government form creation tools have genuine accessibility value — WCAG compliance reduces barriers for disabled users. However, forms are power-distributing artefacts, and a tool that makes it easier to create forms without examining how those forms distribute access is doing implicit power work while claiming technical neutrality. I apply M6 because the design is framed as a technical efficiency improvement without any documented engagement with how form design choices affect which communities can successfully navigate government services.

name: Kagi SlopStop
rationale: M6 applied: AI content detection tool; internet users not excluded populations; for-profit LLC; methodology not fully published as documented limitation

name: CiviClick
rationale: M6 applied: AI-powered advocacy software for public affairs professionals; professionals not excluded populations; for-profit model; no community governance

name: django-collaborative
rationale: M6 applied: technical tip-gathering tool framing without governance/participation dimension

name: User Research Library
rationale: The local government user research library aggregates research conducted about service users — an evidence base for service improvement. But the evidence is used by service designers and policymakers rather than being accessible to the communities whose needs are being researched; there is no mechanism for community contestability of the research findings.

name: Pastecal
rationale: Calendar sharing tool; limited equity or political relevance; primarily technical utility

name: Idealist
rationale: Nonprofit job board; limited structural equity analysis or community empowerment

name: The Guide to Major Trusts 2025/26
rationale: A directory of grant-makers for charities and nonprofits is useful sector infrastructure, but it addresses an information asymmetry within the professional nonprofit sector rather than a power asymmetry affecting communities. The beneficiaries are fundraisers and budget-holders, not the communities served by funded organisations.

name: Teaching Public Service in the Digital Age
rationale: Open-access training for public servants to develop digital-era skills has systemic value — better-trained public servants may design more equitable services. But the direct beneficiaries are educators and public officials, and there is no documented engagement with whether the curriculum addresses how digital service design can exclude communities.

name: Schema.org
rationale: Schema.org defines how information is structured on the internet — infrastructure that shapes who can be found and represented in machine-readable ways. The M6 reduction reflects the purely technical framing of a governance-heavy problem: how schemas encode assumptions about people, organisations, and events has political consequences the Schema.org process does not examine.

name: Overton
rationale: Overton indexes how policy ideas spread and connects researchers with policymakers — a market intelligence tool for people already inside the policy ecosystem. The beneficiary population (policy researchers, think tanks, IGOs) is the opposite of structurally excluded.

name: Registers and Collaboration: Making Lists We Can Trust
rationale: This ODI report on data register governance is valuable technical guidance for practitioners. It sits in the background infrastructure layer of civic data and doesn't engage with who is excluded from the data systems whose governance it discusses, or how register design embeds assumptions about whose existence needs to be formally recorded.

name: GOV.UK Pay
rationale: Payment processing infrastructure for public services reduces costs and standardizes citizen transactions with government. The score reflects functional public sector infrastructure without structural power asymmetry correction — the beneficiaries are primarily government agencies, and there is no documented examination of how payment systems exclude populations without bank accounts or digital access.

name: Papertree
rationale: Tree planting data transparency for climate accountability — a sparse dossier prevents full assessment. Climate accountability tools that primarily serve organizations and researchers without examining the communities most affected by deforestation score limited on my C2 criteria.

name: PatCit
rationale: M6 applied: purely technical patent citation dataset; no governance engagement

name: The DAO (Standard DAO Framework)
rationale: M6 applied: technical smart contract mechanism without adequate governance analysis

name: GRIM (Global Risk Simulator)
rationale: M6 applied: technical simulation framing with no governance dimension

name: Prolific
rationale: Research data collection infrastructure with some documented use in AI governance (Collective Intelligence Project). I apply M4 weakly because the aggregation of participant data for AI training research involves governance questions about whose voices are collected, how, and for whom — the self-selection bias and cost barriers acknowledged in the limitations confirm that the participant pool is not representative of the populations most affected by AI governance decisions.

name: Polimorphic
rationale: AI platform for government operations and resident engagement with case study claims (50% call reduction in Littleton, CO) but no independently verified methodology. I apply both M4 (AI in public services without accountability) and M6 (technical framing bypassing governance) because the proprietary platform obscures how AI is translating resident input into government decisions, and the framing as 'service-first government operations' treats what is fundamentally a political question as a technical efficiency problem.

name: AI Safety Info
rationale: M6 applied: technical AI safety FAQ for researchers/students; generic professional audience; Open Philanthropy/FLI funding; no governance analysis or community empowerment

name: Responsible Tech Guide 2025
rationale: M6 applied: annual informational guide for tech sector professionals; generic professional audience; no community engagement or excluded population focus

name: UK Elections Leaflets
rationale: M6 applied: technical hackathon data project without community engagement

name: PoliMonitor
rationale: Political monitoring for public affairs professionals is a service for organizations that want to track political discussions — essentially B2B political intelligence. The beneficiaries are communications and public affairs professionals, not communities excluded from political processes.

name: Local Insight
rationale: Local data intelligence; limited excluded population focus or participatory design

name: CAN/DGSI 127 Age Assurance Standard
rationale: M6 applied: technical Canadian standards document; developers/policymakers as users; government-funded; no community participation or excluded population focus

name: Choose a License
rationale: M6 applied: technical open source license chooser; developers as users; GitHub-operated; no political or civic governance dimension

name: Manifold Markets
rationale: M6 applied: market mechanism framing treats civic information as tradeable commodity

name: GOV.UK Service Manual
rationale: The Service Standard and Service Manual establish UK government digital service quality norms — including accessibility and user-centred design. I apply M6 weakly because the manual frames good service design as primarily a technical standard ('meeting the 14 points') without examining how design choices distribute access across different communities or how the procurement and political context shapes what services get built for whom.

name: Public Media Stack
rationale: The Public Media Stack maps software tools used in public media workflows — a static inventory resource guide for media organisations. The 2020 launch date and 100-product scope make this a frozen inventory rather than an active power intervention. It exclusively serves media organisations rather than the communities whose stories are or are not told.

name: soweego
rationale: soweego links Wikidata to external catalogs — open data infrastructure maintenance. The apparent inactivity since 2021 and narrow technical scope reflect a tool with no civic power asymmetry dimension and a limited, technical audience.

name: GOV.UK Notify
rationale: Government notification infrastructure — emails, texts, letters — is functional public sector tooling. The score reflects its purely informational function: Notify enables government agencies to communicate decisions to citizens without providing any mechanism for citizens to contest those decisions. The one-directional flow is itself a power distribution choice that the tool does not examine.

name: oTree
rationale: Open-source behavioral research infrastructure for economists and psychologists. The civic relevance is indirect — research on voter behavior and public goods may inform policy. The direct beneficiaries are academics, not communities.

name: Urbit
rationale: Personal server operating system for digital self-sovereignty — technically interesting but the beneficiaries are developers and technology enthusiasts who require significant technical expertise to use it. I apply M6 because the technical framing of sovereignty does not engage with the governance dimensions of who can achieve it or what structural conditions would make it accessible.

name: Gov Reuse Library
rationale: M6 applied: government internal technical reuse library; government developers not excluded populations; MoJ-funded; no community empowerment

name: whatsmeow
rationale: M6 applied: technical WhatsApp API library; no political or governance dimension

name: GreenPT
rationale: M6 applied: technical environmental/privacy framing without governance analysis

name: GOV.UK One Login
rationale: Centralized government identity authentication raises concerns that dominate the positive access-enabling function. I apply M4 strongly because centralizing government identity data across all services substantially increases institutional surveillance capacity without commensurate contestability rights for citizens, and I apply M2 partially because 'streamlined access' framing obscures how the platform increases government visibility into citizen service use.

name: PolicyMogul
rationale: PolicyMogul is a commercial public affairs monitoring tool for people already embedded in the policy process. The for-profit model and professional user base place it at the far end from the concerns this constitution prioritises; policy access tools that serve paid professionals score much lower than those serving communities without institutional representation.

name: Understanding Your Morality
rationale: Understanding Your Morality is an individual values clarification tool from Clearer Thinking. There is no community, no power asymmetry, no excluded population, and no democratic depth dimension; it is a self-assessment quiz with no structural civic function.

name: WorkInCharities
rationale: A job board for the charity sector — useful professional infrastructure but with no structural relevance to power asymmetries, excluded populations, or democratic participation.

name: Bluesky Social
rationale: M6 applied: predominantly technical decentralisation framing; HIGH pop_risk: platform infrastructure without equity mandate

name: postcodes.io
rationale: M6 applied: geographic API technical framing; no community empowerment dimension

name: Empurrando Juntas (EJ)
rationale: Empurrando Juntas's AI-powered opinion collection with persona segmentation raises the exact concerns from my Open Banking and SKEPSIS work: framing data collection about communities as participation while the data product (audience personas) primarily benefits institutions wanting to understand and communicate with those communities. The absence of documented community control over how segmentation data is used triggers both M2 and M4.

name: Esper
rationale: M6 applied: proprietary AI-assisted government platform; government agencies not excluded populations; no documented limitations; commercial orientation with no community governance

name: GovWise
rationale: AI procurement tender screening for businesses — B2B commercial tool for organizations participating in public procurement. I apply M6 weakly because the framing of procurement as an AI efficiency problem obscures the governance question of which businesses get access to public contracts and how procurement decisions affect public services.

name: Whoisology
rationale: Archived WHOIS domain records searchable by corporate intelligence and cybersecurity teams — M4 applies because this increases institutional capacity to aggregate data about individuals' online activities without commensurate governance structures giving those individuals contestability rights.

name: Awesome Gov Datasets
rationale: M6 applied: purely technical government data catalog; CDDO/government-internal framing

name: Journalist Studio
rationale: M6 applied: technical Google platform framing; commercial orientation reduces structural equity value

name: OpenAudience
rationale: OpenAudience's postcode-based audience profiling for political campaigners increases institutional capacity to target communities without giving those communities any mechanism to understand or contest how they are being classified and communicated with. This is the exact profiling-without-governance pattern M4 penalises; framing postcode demographic analysis as open data empowerment when it primarily serves political targeting also invites M2 scrutiny.

name: Fission Codes
rationale: M6 applied: purely technical Web3 status codes; no civic or governance dimension

name: Granicus
rationale: M6 applied: purely commercial technical platform for government communication; no community empowerment

name: Yoti
rationale: Biometric identity platform framing facial recognition and age estimation as trusted empowerment — M2 applies strongly because the 'trusted identity' framing enables expanded institutional profiling of individuals through biometric data without genuine community control, and M4 applies because facial recognition accuracy disparities across demographics represent governance failures that the platform's independent testing claim does not adequately resolve.
